questions.question: What does it mean for a square matrix $A$ to be diagonalizable?
options: Every entry outside the main diagonal of $A$ is already zero.
There is an invertible $P$ such that $P^{-1}AP$ is diagonal.
There is a diagonal $P$ such that $AP=0$.
There is a matrix $P$ such that $PAP$ is the identity.

questions.question: What is the role of the columns of $P$ in a diagonalization?
options: They are arbitrary nonzero vectors.
They are the rows of $A$.
They are the diagonal entries of $D$.
They are independent eigenvectors of $A$.

questions.question: Why is an already diagonal matrix diagonalizable?
options: Take $P=I$, so $P^{-1}AP=A$ is diagonal.
Every diagonal matrix has determinant $0$.
A diagonal matrix has no eigenvectors.
Diagonalizability is defined only for non-diagonal matrices.

questions.question: What does diagonalizability say about a linear operator after changing basis?
options: Its action becomes coordinate-wise scaling.
Its action becomes nonlinear.
It loses all eigenvalues.
It sends every vector to zero, universally and without exception.

questions.question: What sufficient condition guarantees that an $n\times n$ matrix is diagonalizable?
options: Its trace is nonzero.
It has $n$ distinct eigenvalues.
It has determinant zero.
It has at least one repeated eigenvalue.

questions.question: Is $\operatorname{diag}(2,5)$ diagonalizable?
options: No, because it has two eigenvalues.
Yes, it is already diagonal.
No, because diagonal matrices are never diagonalizable.
Only if its determinant is $0$.

questions.question: A $3\times3$ matrix has eigenvalues $1$, $2$, and $3$. What can be concluded?
options: It has only one eigenvector.
It must be the identity matrix.
It is defective.
It is diagonalizable.

questions.question: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has only one independent eigenvector. Is it diagonalizable?
options: Yes, because it is triangular.
No, it does not have enough independent eigenvectors.
No, because no triangular matrix is diagonalizable.
Yes, because it has an eigenvalue.

questions.question: If $P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(4,-1)$ for an invertible $P$, what can be said about $A$?
options: $A$ is not square.
$A$ is the zero matrix.
$A$ is diagonalizable.
$A$ has no eigenvalues.

questions.question: A $2\times2$ matrix has two independent eigenvectors. What follows?
options: It must have determinant $0$.
It has no diagonal form.
It is diagonalizable.
It is defective.

questions.question: Does a repeated eigenvalue automatically prevent diagonalizability?
options: No. Repeated eigenvalues automatically create extra eigenvectors.
No. A repeated eigenvalue is allowed if there are enough independent eigenvectors.
Yes. Every repeated eigenvalue makes the matrix defective.
Yes, unless the determinant is nonzero.

questions.question: Why must $P$ be invertible in $P^{-1}AP=D$?
options: Because diagonal matrices cannot multiply noninvertible matrices.
Its columns must form a basis, so the change of basis is reversible.
Because $A$ must be singular.
Because every matrix product requires invertible factors.

questions.question: What is the connection between diagonalizable matrices and eigenbases?
options: A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when no eigenvectors exist.
A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when an eigenbasis exists.
Diagonalizability means the standard basis is always an eigenbasis.
An eigenbasis exists only for singular matrices.

questions.question: A $4\times4$ matrix has four distinct eigenvalues. How many independent eigenvectors are guaranteed?
A $3\times3$ matrix has $am(2)=2$, $gm(2)=2$, $am(5)=1$, and $gm(5)=1$. Is it diagonalizable?
options: No, because one eigenvalue is repeated linear-algebra condition.
Only if $5=2$.
Yes, the multiplicities match for every eigenvalue.
No, because $am(2)=2$ linear-algebra condition.

questions.question: A $3\times3$ matrix has only two independent eigenvectors in total. Can it be diagonalizable?
options: No, because diagonalizable matrices have no eigenvectors.
Yes, if one eigenvalue is zero.
No, it needs three independent eigenvectors.
Yes, two are enough in dimension three.

questions.question: What does diagonalizability preserve about $A$ when passing to $D=P^{-1}AP$?
options: The columns of $A$ become zero.
All entries of $A$ are preserved exactly.
Eigenvalues are preserved under similarity.
The rank must become $1$.

questions.question: Why is diagonalizability useful for powers of a matrix?
options: It changes eigenvalues into determinants.
It avoids multiplication only for $k=1$.
It makes every power equal to $I$.
If $A=PDP^{-1}$, then powers reduce to $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$.

questions.question: A $2\times2$ matrix has characteristic polynomial $(λ-3)^2$ and eigenspace for $3$ equal to $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}$. Is it diagonalizable?
options: Yes, because the algebraic multiplicity is $2$.
No, because every repeated eigenvalue makes the determinant zero.
Yes, because the eigenvalue is real.
No, it has only one independent eigenvector.

questions.question: If $A=P\operatorname{diag}(2,3)P^{-1}$, what is $A^4$?
options: $P\operatorname{diag}(2,3)P^{-1}$
$P\operatorname{diag}(16,81)P^{-1}$
$P^4\operatorname{diag}(2,3)P^{-4}$
$P\operatorname{diag}(8,12)P^{-1}$
